idiom_name: Result<T> (success T | failure Throwable) with runCatching/fold/getOrElse
implementation_notes: Kotlin's standard library ships Result<T>, a value class that is either a success with a T or a failure with an arbitrary Throwable; runCatching { } turns a throwing lambda into a Result, and fold, map/mapCatching, recover, getOrElse, getOrNull, onSuccess and onFailure consume it. It is the stdlib's answer to the failure contract and needs no dependency, but the failure type is fixed to Throwable, so a domain error must be modelled as an exception subclass (or carried inside the success payload) if callers are to branch on structured reasons - the limitation that motivates the Arrow variant. Prefer runCatching at the boundary where third-party code throws, and explicit Result.success/Result.failure at your own edges.
pitfalls: The failure is a Throwable, not a domain value: exception subclasses used as error cases still carry stack traces and their messages are not part of the contract.
Result is designed as a return-value type; using it as a field type or a type argument can hit the value-class restrictions and need wrapper workarounds.
runCatching catches everything, including cancellation-style control flow; rethrow what is not a real failure.

variants.name: Arrow Either (typed errors)
variants.implementation_notes: Arrow's core type is Either<Error, Value>: the failure branch carries whatever domain type is declared, with no Throwable requirement, and the either { } builder with the Raise<E> receiver lets a function declare its error type and call bind() on each step, short-circuiting on the first failure. Its documentation frames this exactly as typed logical failures versus real exceptions and provides explicit recovery and accumulation helpers. It is the library form for teams that treat domain failures as data and keep exceptions for genuine faults; the cost is a functional-programming dependency and the Raise DSL to learn, while kotlin.Result stays the zero-dependency default.
variants.idiom_name: Either<E, A> with the either { } / Raise<E> DSL
pitfalls: Two error models coexist (kotlin.Result and Either); pick one per module boundary and convert, or every call site guesses which wrapper is in play.
bind() only short-circuits inside either { }/recover blocks - calling it elsewhere is a compile error that newcomers hit immediately.
